comments.text:
REPRODUCTION ATTEMPTED AND REFUSED — INCONCLUSIVE, plus a bounded STATIC reading offered as two candidate mechanisms and the measurement that would separate them. Nothing here is a diagnosis and nothing here is a reproduction.

REPRODUCTION: npm run test:chrome on a clean checkout of CURRENT MAIN 5e5fd815 (build:production rc=0, check:dist clean) exited 75 after the gate's full 601229 ms quiet-window bound. CAP_ENVIRONMENTAL_REFUSAL {"load1":32.42,"load5":28.32,"load15":20.36,"cores":32,"loadPerCore":1.013125,"compilers":6,"compilerNames":["esbuild"],"measurable":true,"activeCompilers":3}. Zero PASS/FAIL lines: the refusal precedes browser start. Samples across the wait never approached the threshold (0.47, 0.72, 0.64, 0.74, 1.13, 1.29, 0.99, 0.84, 0.67, 0.61, 0.66, 1.09, 0.96, 0.90, then 1.01 at refusal), and dnop's active count named 3 genuinely compiling esbuild processes, so this was real build activity rather than parked services. The box was ~3x the load threshold, not marginally over. NOT RETRIED: this bead's claim is about an idle box (its own evidence reads load/core=0.19) and load15 is 20.36, so a window is not imminent; a retry now either refuses again or produces a 132/370 indistinguishable from load, which is the misattribution 9t1p was filed to stop. So the question "did 35o1 or a later landing already fix the enqueue?" REMAINS OPEN and is not answered by source reading. Evidence: ~/cap-evidence/jnwb-repro/{main-5e5fd815.log,driver.log}.

STATIC READING of runScriptedToolProbe (scripts/chrome-journeys.ts:525-570 at 5e5fd815), offered as two candidates because both are consistent with the observed "0 of 5 requests, phase no durable run record" and I cannot separate them without a run:

CANDIDATE A — the two driver steps that start the run have their RESULTS DISCARDED.
    await typeInto(cdp, ntpSession, "#task-input", task);
    await clickSel(cdp, ntpSession, "#run-task");
Neither return value is read. typeInto returns false when clickSel cannot resolve a point, and clickSel returns false when boxOf yields null — so a typing failure or a missed Run click presents EXACTLY as the reported symptom: the provider receives 0 requests, no durable run record is created, and the probe waits its full 120 s before reporting a shortfall that names the provider rather than the step that never happened. Note these still use the retired composer ids; they resolve because boxOf (:367-380) carries the compat mapping to [data-composer-input]/[data-composer-send], but that mapping is DOCUMENT-WIDE, so it resolves to whichever composer comes first in document order — and ntp.html carries two (#composer at :1026, #thread-composer at :1233). The probe does click #home first, so the hub composer should be the target; whether it is visible and hittable at that moment is exactly what a discarded return value would hide. This is the same class as 9t1p fixed for the timeout loop and as qdjn fixed for the per-width guards: a silent failure reporting as a different, more confusing failure.

CANDIDATE B — the probe's agent.run never gets dispatched because a PRIOR run in the same block is still in flight. The comment immediately above the cookie-probe call site (:~4060) says: "Leaving the run paused here is what hung the suite (the next agent.run queued behind it until the CDP evaluate timed out), so the card is ALWAYS settled before moving on." So this block has a known history of a paused run blocking the next enqueue. If the settling step did not complete, the probe's run would queue and never start — producing the same 0-of-5 and the same absent durable record.

WHAT WOULD SEPARATE THEM, in one quiet-window run: capture the return values of the two driver steps and the in-flight run set at probe start. If typeInto/clickSel return false, it is A. If both return true and a prior executionId is still non-terminal when the probe types, it is B. Both observations are cheap and neither weakens the shortfall assertion, which must stay exactly as strict as it is.

A FIX I AM PROPOSING AND DELIBERATELY NOT SHIPPING: assert the two discarded return values so a failed step is named at the step instead of surfacing 120 s later as a provider shortfall. It is low-risk, changes nothing when the steps succeed, and is the same shape as 9t1p's three-outcomes change. I am not shipping it because I cannot verify it — any change to this gate needs a quiet-window drive to prove it did not move the 132/370 for an unrelated reason, and coord's ordering is reproduce first. Shipping an unverifiable change to the strongest gate is the thing I have declined all session.

NO ATTRIBUTION IS MADE. Per cap-astra's caution, which I am adopting as the standard for this bead: a quiet sample is a control, not a cause, and "0 requests / no durable record" is an observed CHECKPOINT, not a root cause. Both candidates above are consistent with the observation and neither is established.

comments.author: Paul Kinlan
comments.text:
STATIC ROOT-CAUSE CANDIDATE, found before being re-tasked to 32yz. Releasing the claim; this is where I stopped and what is measured. NOT driven in a browser, so it is a candidate, not a confirmed cause.

THE MECHANISM: boxOf() (scripts/chrome-journeys.ts) returns getBoundingClientRect() UNFILTERED, so a HIDDEN element yields {x:0,y:0} rather than null. clickSel() then dispatches a real mouse click at the viewport origin and RETURNS TRUE. typeInto() proceeds to type into whatever has focus (nothing). So the probe's three input steps — clickSel('#home'), typeInto('#task-input', task), clickSel('#run-task') — can all report success while nothing was clicked and no run was ever enqueued. That is exactly jnwb's signature: 0 of 5 provider requests, phase 'no durable run record', and the full 136 s wait.

EXECUTABLE REPRODUCTION (no browser; source-extracts the REAL helpers with new Function and drives them against a fake CDP, the house pattern from tests/journey-cdp-timeout.test.ts). Script retained at /tmp/jnwb-probe.mjs:
  boxOf(hidden element)  = {"x":0,"y":0}
  clickSel(hidden)       = true   -> dispatched at ["0,0","0,0"]
  boxOf(absent element)  = null
  clickSel(absent)       = false
The ABSENT case is handled; the HIDDEN case is not. A zero-rect click fails identically however long you wait, which matches the bead's own note that a 7m29s run and an 8m run both died at the same place — i.e. not a timing race at this level.

TWO WAYS THE HUB COMPOSER CAN BE NON-INTERACTABLE THERE, both measured statically: (1) extension/ntp/ntp.html:1194 declares #thread-view as a class="view-overlay" that can cover the hub; (2) ntp.html carries TWO agent-composer elements (#composer at :1033 and #thread-composer at :1240), so the probe's UNSCOPED '#task-input' resolves via boxOf's compat mapping to whichever [data-composer-input] comes first in document order rather than to the hub's. AgentComposer is light DOM (static shadow() { return false; }), so both hooks are reachable to document.querySelector — which is why this resolves to the wrong element rather than failing loudly.

PROPOSED FIX SHAPE (not implemented): make boxOf FAIL CLOSED on a zero/degenerate rect and on an element that is not hit-testable at its own centre point, returning null so clickSel reports false exactly as the absent case already does; and scope the probe's composer selectors to the hub host so two composers cannot resolve ambiguously. The falsification is cheap and inverted — the MUTANT is today's behaviour: restore the unfiltered rect and the reproduction above returns true at 0,0 again.

WHAT I DID NOT DO, stated plainly: no npm run test:chrome drive. The box measured load 19.23 (30.58 five-minute) on 32 cores while I was on this, and the journey gate is load-sensitive by its own registry declaration — 9t1p exists because a run under load produces a verdict about the box, not the tree. So the driven half of this bead is OWED, and the static finding above must not be read as confirming the 132/370 cause until someone drives it in a quiet window. Also unverified: whether making boxOf strict lets the keyless/cookie block REACH its checks, or merely fails earlier with a better message — jnwb's acceptance requires the former, and that distinction needs the driven run to settle.

comments.text: coord 04:28Z — EVIDENCE FOR THIS BEAD'S OWNERSHIP QUESTION, from a change that could not use the gate. While landing chrome-agent-platform-3337 (which rewrites emitted code in ALL TWELVE bundles by removing a shared process.env define module), the only leg that can catch a boot-time ReferenceError in the service worker is a real extension load — and j5yz measured that NO RUNNABLE SUBSET OF THIS GATE EXISTS: scripts/chrome-journeys.ts (9,401 lines) is the only path that loads the extension, its only argument is --retain (line 18), and the checks that would serve as a smoke ('extension loaded', 'SW attach returned a session id', 'SW Runtime.enable succeeded', 'initial SW boot observed via pre-attached restart') are items INSIDE the 370-check list (lines 650-658), not a runnable subset. Greps for Deno.args handling, CAP_*JOURNEY, SMOKE and BOOT_SMOKE return nothing. The nearest near-smoke, scripts/component-gallery-smoke.ts, does not load the extension at all (launchChrome with no loadExtension), so it cannot observe a boot-time SW failure. CONSEQUENCE, which is a real and recurring cost rather than a one-off: ANY change touching emitted bundle code has exactly two options — a 45-minute owner-window browser run of all 370 checks, or landing with the boot path UNVERIFIED and a named rollback. Tonight that forced the second option on a plumbing change with strong executed and static coverage, and it is the same reason the project's own loaded-extension acceptance has stayed open. PROPOSED ACCEPTANCE for this bead (and coord will split it into its own bead if Paul prefers it separate): add either (a) a --only/--check selector to chrome-journeys.ts so the four boot checks above can run alone in a bounded window, or (b) a dedicated extension-boot smoke that does loadExtension and asserts only that boot and SW attach succeed — so that every future bundle-touching change can verify a real boot cheaply instead of choosing between 45 minutes and blind. coord is not claiming this bead (it is Paul's) and is recording this as evidence plus a concrete deliverable rather than a complaint.

title: Two landed tests measure the box: the fleet-slot test assumes a free slot, the compiler test lets ambient load cause its refusal
description:
Two of my own landed tests are not hermetic to a busy box, found when npm test on the rshb branch ran at load1 20.9 / load5 43.4 with another lane's real journey gate active. Neither red is caused by rshb (that tree was green at 4437/0 in npm run test:changed minutes earlier); both are the "a test that measures the box as well as the code" class the 2026-09-23 review named, and both are in branches that already landed:

1. tests/heavy-gate-slot.test.ts — "0lj3: a HELD fleet slot makes the REAL journey gate refuse, naming the holder, and start no browser" (tests/heavy-gate-slot.test.ts:277).
   Observed: HeavyGateSlotRefusedError — "the fleet-wide heavy-gate slot is busy (waited 2009 ms) — held by chrome-journeys (pid 3128320 …)".
   Cause: the test HOLDS the real fleet slot /tmp/cap-heavy-gate.lock and then expects the real journey gate to refuse. If another lane's journey gate already holds it, the TEST's own hold is refused, so the test reds. The mechanism is correct — two gates must not share the machine — and the test assumes a free fleet slot.
   Acceptance: the test acquires the held slot with a bounded retry (or reports an explicit SKIP-with-reason that names the foreign holder), so a concurrent real gate cannot red it, while the assertion (the real journey gate refuses and starts no browser) is unchanged and still proved when the slot is free. Do NOT weaken the assertion to "it refused for some reason" — the property is that the holder is named.

2. tests/quiet-window.test.ts — "mkax: the REAL journey gate refuses with exit 75 while a REAL compiler is compiling (dnop)" (tests/quiet-window.test.ts:561).
   Observed refusal payload: {"load1":25.39,"loadPerCore":0.79,"compilers":12,"activeCompilers":0,"measurable":true} — the refusal came from the box's LOAD, not from the test's burner, and the test asserts activeCompilers >= 1.
   Cause: the spawned gate's env pins CAP_QUIET_WAIT_MS / SAMPLE_MS / MAX_COMPILERS / SUSTAINED but NOT CAP_QUIET_MAX_LOAD_PER_CORE, so on a loaded box the load condition alone causes the refusal. The test can then neither prove its own property nor fail honestly — and worse, on a slightly less loaded box it could pass for the load reason rather than the compile reason.
   Acceptance: pin CAP_QUIET_MAX_LOAD_PER_CORE high (the startup-failure drill already does this with maxLoadPerCore: 100) so ONLY the compile condition can produce the refusal; then the existing assertion (the refusal payload reports a compiling builder) is exactly the property. Falsification: remove the burner and the gate must NOT refuse.
close_reason: Landed on origin/main as v0.3.462 at commit 61e4fdabef7752f48df1737e674d806bee3fe75b. Private slot paths for contention tests prevent collision with live fleet gate locks.

comments.author: Paul Kinlan
comments.text:
PATTERN, stated plainly as coord asked (this is the generalisation, not the two instances):

**A test whose SUBJECT is contention, written without accounting for the contention the fleet creates by existing.** Both failures are that one shape:
• tests/quiet-window.test.ts attributed a refusal to its own deliberate burner while ambient LOAD was the real cause — the payload it printed said so and it read past it: {"load1":25.39,"loadPerCore":0.79,"compilers":12,"activeCompilers":0}.
• tests/heavy-gate-slot.test.ts assumed a free fleet slot while a real journey gate held it.
The tell is in both messages: the test's own evidence names the foreign cause, and the assertion blames the local one. Same defect as voicebox's gate tonight, one level up: an instrument that cannot distinguish "my input caused this" from "the world caused this" will report whichever it was told to expect.

FIXES (acceptance already in the description; the shape of each):
1. heavy-gate-slot.test.ts: take a PRIVATE slot path for the test's own hold and pass CAP_HEAVY_GATE_SLOT=<the same private path> to the spawned journey gate, so the test neither collides with a real gate nor blocks one. The assertion stays exact (the refusal names the fixture holder and no browser starts).
2. quiet-window.test.ts: pin CAP_QUIET_MAX_LOAD_PER_CORE high in the spawned gate's env so ONLY the compile condition can cause the refusal — the startup-failure drill already does exactly this with maxLoadPerCore: 100. Falsification: with the pin removed, the same test at load1>11 reds for the load reason; with it, the compile is the only possible cause.

comments.author: Paul Kinlan
comments.text:
LANDED: fix/zeew-hermetic-tests @ 2a302db20bbd3775734e2dc4e111b0067b31b508 (remote verified). Version 0.3.460 — NOTE FOR THE MERGER: chrome-agent-platform-rshb (fix/rshb-pad-left-shorthand @ 0c77c288) is ALSO 0.3.460, both branched from main's 0.3.459; whichever lands second needs renumbering.

GATE: npm test at this tip is GREEN — 16 serial + 474 parallel files, 490 total, 4431 passed / 0 failed / 1 ignored, wall 237 s. All three failures from the rshb-tip run are gone, including tests/serial-phase-resilience.test.ts (which did not reproduce at this load — see the note below).

THE DIAGNOSIS IN THIS BEAD WAS HALF WRONG, AND THE DRILL CORRECTED IT — recorded because the wrong half is instructive:
• The bead proposed pinning CAP_QUIET_MAX_LOAD_PER_CORE as the fix for the compiler test. I implemented it, ran the mutant, and the mutant SURVIVED — the pin is necessary-but-not-sufficient.
• The real mechanism was fleet-slot contention, visible in the failure's own duration: the test took 7m29s because the gate it spawns takes the fleet-wide slot BEFORE it measures, so it queued behind another lane's real journey gate. By the time it measured, its own burners (40 × 3 s compiles) had exited — so the refusal came from the box's load with activeCompilers 0, the payload the assertion cannot satisfy.
• Same root cause in the other test, from the other side: it held the REAL slot to prove the journey gate refuses while held, so a real gate made the TEST's hold fail ("held by chrome-journeys (pid 3128320)").
So both tests assumed the fleet's own gate slot was free. The primary fix in each is a PRIVATE slot path; the load pin stays as a secondary guard, and a bounded slot wait means a future mistake fails in seconds rather than in 20 minutes.

VERIFIED PAIRS (ambient conditions deliberately worse than the failing run: a live foreign holder on the REAL slot, load1 23.19 = 0.72/core):
• heavy-gate-slot.test.ts — fixed: PASS in 2 s; mutant (real path, same holder): RED naming foreign-holder-drill.
• quiet-window.test.ts — fixed: PASS in 8 s (was 7m29s FAIL at a lower load); mutant (no private slot, holder alive): RED in 14 s refusing {"reason":"heavy-gate-slot-busy","holder":{"gate":"foreign-holder-drill",…}} — it refuses for the SLOT reason, not the compile reason, which is exactly what the assertion exists to catch.
My load generators were bounded and mine (16 CPU burners, 100–120 s, stopped); the foreign holder is a fixture on the real slot for 150 s.

STILL OPEN, filed separately: tests/serial-phase-resilience.test.ts "pozs: timed-out serial file leaves no descendant processes behind" failed once with "grandchild pid must have been recorded" at load1 20.9 / load5 43.4 and did NOT reproduce on the green run — a load-sensitive fixture with a timing assumption, not one of the two fixed here.

description: Independent 0lj3 review at 5fb8d954: scripts/lib/heavy-gate-slot.ts:40 declares /tmp/cap-heavy-gate.holder.json and readHeavyGateHolder defaults there, but slotPaths:95 writes /tmp/cap-heavy-gate.lock.holder.json. The described fix (default reader path agrees with the slot's announced sidecar; no constant-vs-written-path mismatch) is present in main scripts/lib/heavy-gate-slot.ts:100-106 (private slot overrides stay isolated), carried by 9811e07cc. The foreign branch fix/n772-one-sidecar-path@0dae9c74 was NOT the carrier and is left untouched.

comments.author: Paul Kinlan
comments.text:
FIXED AND PUSHED — `fix/n772-one-sidecar-path` @ `0dae9c74`, with one honest correction to the bead's premise and one new defect found in the same observable.

**1. THE REPORTED PATH MISMATCH IS ALREADY FIXED ON MAIN — verified by execution, not by reading the file.** `heavyGateHolderPathFor(HEAVY_GATE_SLOT_PATH) === HEAVY_GATE_HOLDER_PATH` (the pure agreement), and a real acquisition followed by `readHeavyGateHolder()` **with no path argument** names the live holder: `n772-probe (pid 1117647, alive=true)`. On disk only `/tmp/cap-heavy-gate.holder.json` exists — there is no `cap-heavy-gate.lock.holder.json` anywhere. The default-case special-case came in with the 0lj3 revision, so the bead's description matches the **pre-revision** code (`slotPaths:95` reading `${slotPath}.holder.json` unconditionally). Recorded rather than silently delivering a no-op fix.

**2. WHAT WAS GENUINELY MISSING, and is the substance of the change: the tests that would have caught it.** The existing checks compared the exported constant to a literal, and the live round trip used a *private* slot with a path computed by the same function under test — neither exercises "the writer's announcement for the DEFAULT slot is visible to the DEFAULT reader". Added three drills:
- **n772-a**: the pure agreement PLUS an executing default-path check — acquire the real default slot only if it is free (300 ms bound, so it can never hold a real gate up), then read through the **default reader**. If another lane holds the slot it prints an explicit **INCONCLUSIVE** line rather than passing quietly, and it never waits for the fleet slot.
- **n772-b**: private-slot isolation — the announcement lands beside its own slot; the default path's bytes are identical before and after; the default reader never names the private holder.
- **n772-c**: see (3).

**3. A SECOND DEFECT, MEASURED WHILE VERIFYING THIS ONE.** Acquiring a **FREE** slot fired `onWait` once with:
  `heavy-gate: free-slot-probe waiting for the fleet-wide gate slot [...] (bound 2000 ms) — held by an unnamed holder (no announcement sidecar)`
while the acquisition completed in **~8 ms** — a holder claim **where there was no holder**. Consequence: real contention was indistinguishable from an uncontended acquisition in every gate's log (this lane misread that line repeatedly during the 2026-09-23 gate work, and it appears in this repo's own gate logs). Cause: the line was printed at the TOP of the first loop iteration, before any read. Fix: announce only after a **200 ms grace** with a **fresh** holder read (so the lane that actually holds it is named), and poll the read at **250 ms** so the loop can reach that point at all while still respecting the bound — a read that blocks for the whole deadline never gets a second chance to speak. A genuinely held slot still names its holder correctly: `held by the-real-holder (pid 1121876, started …)`.

comments.author: Paul Kinlan
comments.text:
FIXED AND PUSHED — `fix/o3rx-flock-setup-vs-contention` @ `f0959578` (off main `d31158b0`).

**1. THE REVIEWED CASE IS ALREADY CORRECT ON THIS TREE — verified by execution.** The review's bad-path probe (a lock path under a missing directory) now yields `HeavyGateSlotSetupError`, not `HeavyGateSlotRefusedError`: measured `missing parent dir (the reviewer's bad-path): HeavyGateSlotSetupError — ENVIRONMENT: … could not be SET UP at …`. The 0lj3 revision added that classification, so the review at `5fb8d954` describes the pre-revision code — as with n772, recorded plainly rather than shipping a no-op.

**2. WHAT THE CLASSIFICATION STILL GOT WRONG, which is what this change fixes.** The discriminator was a **message scan** (`/cannot open lock file|Permission denied|No such file or directory/` or exit 66). Measured flock behaviour (util-linux, 2026-09-24) shows why that cannot be the rule:
| shape | exit | stderr |
|---|---|---|
| contention (held, `-w` elapsed) | **1** | **empty** |
| missing parent / permission / read-only fs | 66 | `cannot open lock file …` |
| invalid timeout value | 64 | `invalid timeout: 'abc'` |
| cannot execute the command | 69 | `failed to execute …` |
| helper killed (OOM or the backstop) | `status.code = null` | signal `SIGKILL` |
So contention is **a quiet exit 1** — or a helper our own backstop killed while it was still waiting — and everything else is a setup/system fault. The old rule still classified a helper that **never performed the handshake** (silent exit 0, or any code it did not recognise, e.g. a stub/wrapper `flock` resolved from PATH, or a signal-killed helper) as *"the slot is busy, held by an unnamed holder"*: a peer blamed for something that was not contention, the exact inverse of this file's own note that "reporting a setup fault as busy sends a lane to wait for a holder that does not exist".

**3. CHANGE.** `contention = (exit === 1 && stderr === "") || (status.code === null && signal === SIGKILL)`; otherwise `HeavyGateSlotSetupError` carrying flock's own **bounded (300 char)** words plus its exit status or signal — the "retain bounded diagnostics/status" half of the acceptance.

**4. TESTS (executing, each staging a real failure).** `o3rx-a` a helper that cannot execute its command (PATH containing flock but no `sh`) → SETUP naming *"failed to execute"*; `o3rx-b` an unwritable lock directory (chmod 500) → SETUP naming the access failure; `o3rx-c` a helper that never performs the handshake (stub `flock` exiting 0 and 70, silently) → SETUP, never busy, and never naming a peer. Real contention still yields the refusal and names the holder (existing 0lj3 drills).

**5. MUTANTS.** **M1** the previous message-scan rule restored → `o3rx-c` **RED** (silent exit 0 blamed on a peer — the proof this rule is load-bearing); **M2** everything is contention → all three SETUP drills **RED**; **M3** nothing is contention → the two 0lj3 **contention** drills **RED** (so I did not simply make everything a setup error).

**6. GATES.** `npm run test:changed` GREEN on re-run: 19 + 26 + 325 passed, 0 failed. **The first run reddened on an unrelated check — `dqxa: prepareLoadedExtension refuses a pre-existing probe before destination copying or injection` (`tests/emscripten-abi-loaded-harness.test.ts:252`) — because a stale `extension/_emscripten_abi_probe` directory was present in that worktree, which that check refuses BY DESIGN; the exact check passes alone on re-run, and the whole gate was green afterwards.** Worth a separate look: a leftover probe directory from an interrupted run makes *any* unrelated change's `test:changed` red. `npm test` GREEN — 4466 passed / 0 failed / 1 ignored (14 steps).

title: Four-surfaces journey disagrees: sidepanel agents-picker counts ACP harness agents (+3 rows on a fresh profile) — product call on the projection rule
description:
Found reading the l0r browser-run logs (three runs, 8/16/8 assertion failures, logs in ~/cap-evidence/glm-l0r/we0m/journeys-red-attempt{1,2,3}-abort.log): the fresh-profile four-surfaces journey (chrome-journeys 'fresh profile: the four agent surfaces agree (0/1/0) again') fails DETERMINISTICALLY — 3/3 runs — because the side panel's agents-picker now counts ACP harness agents while the other three surfaces do not.

Measured: fresh profile -> hub sidebar 0, hub panel '0 agents · 0 site', Settings 'No agents yet.', SIDEPANEL PICKER 3 rows. With one recipe enabled: others agree at 1, sidepanel 4. The +3 is constant = the three ACP harness agents the registry admits callable-by-default (extension/shared/agent-registry.js: AGENT_KINDS includes 'acp'; 'ACP harness agents are callable unless explicitly disabled').

This is a product/journey expectation conflict introduced by the ACP registry work (8dcb89ce + qlho's 83d33a42), not by the l0r rename. The CAP-FB-20260830-FRESH-PROFILE-TEMPLATE-AGENTS-01 invariant says hub sidebar + hub panel + side panel tab + Settings share ONE projection (created named agents + enabled background agents); the picker rendering acp harness entries breaks the side-panel leg of that invariant — or the invariant legitimately grew a fourth kind and the journey's expectation needs updating. That is an owner/product call:

(a) if harness agents SHOULD appear in the side panel picker: update the journey to count named+background+acp consistently across the four surfaces (and fix the hub/settings projections to agree), or scope the journey's sidepanel count to the non-acp rows;
(b) if they should NOT: gate acp rows in the picker on the same projection rule.

Also in play: does the picker's callable-only attribute intend to filter acp? It evidently does not exclude them.

Acceptance: the fresh-profile journey passes 0/1/0 with the four surfaces genuinely agreeing, and the chosen projection rule is stated in docs where the invariant lives.

comments.author: Paul Kinlan
comments.text:
OWNER-FACING (flagged to coord 2026-09-23 for Paul's ruling — the projection rule is a product decision, not a check repair). The bead carries the measured numbers; the decision in one line:

Should a FRESH profile's sidepanel agents-picker show the three ACP harness agents (pi / Claude / Codex) by default, or should the four agent surfaces project the SAME set (today: hub sidebar 0, hub Agents panel '0 agents · 0 site', Settings 'No agents yet.', sidepanel picker 3 — and 1/1/1/4 after enabling one background agent)?

(a) YES, harness agents belong in the picker: the ONE-projection invariant (CAP-FB-20260830-FRESH-PROFILE-TEMPLATE-AGENTS-01) grows a fourth kind — update the invariant's doc + the journey to count named+background+acp on all four surfaces (hub/settings projections currently exclude acp, so they'd change too).
(b) NO, the picker stays on the created-agents projection: gate acp rows in <agent-picker> (sidepanel.html uses callable-only — it evidently does not exclude acp) behind the same projection rule the other three surfaces use.

Either ruling must land with the journey re-pinned to the chosen truth (it currently fails deterministically 3/3, measured evidence in ~/cap-evidence/glm-l0r/we0m/BROWSER-FAILURE-ANALYSIS.md).

comments.author: Paul Kinlan
comments.text:
MEASUREMENT AND RECOMMENDATION — no fix, no product call. Coord asked for the numbers with each
surface named; they are below, and the mechanism is traced to file:line on current origin/main.

WHAT I DROVE AND WHAT I READ
I did not run a browser tonight: load was 74.7 at the time of writing and the fresh-profile journey
needs both a quiet window and browser authority this lane does not hold. So the counts come from real
fresh-profile runs that already exist — l0r's three abort logs at
~/cap-evidence/glm-l0r/we0m/journeys-red-attempt{1,2,3}-abort.log, which print the journey's own
`measureAgentSurfaces()` object — and the mechanism comes from reading current main. Every number
below is a quote from those logs, not an inference; every code claim is a file:line you can open.

THE NUMBERS. Same three runs, identical each time, and a fourth scenario added:

  surface              selector                                        fresh  1 recipe  disabled  2 agents*
  hub sidebar          #side-agents .agent-item                           0         1         0         2
  hub panel rows       (panelRows, same list re-read)                     0         1         0         2
  hub panel count      #agent-count                          "0 agents ·      "1 agent ·     "0 agents ·"    —
                       (one string with site)                          0 site"      0 site"
  Settings rows        #unified-agent-list .agent-settings-row            0         1         0         2
  side panel picker    #agents-picker · shadowRoot · .opt                 3         4         3         5

  * the scheduled-template scenario at chrome-journeys.ts:2553, which asserts sidebar/panel/settings
    at 2 each and does NOT assert the picker — see finding 3. It is the fourth column.

The delta is a constant +3 on the picker in every scenario, and it is exactly
`"pi,claude-code:Claude Code,codex:Codex".split(",")` at service-worker.js:7831. Red assertions, all
three, verbatim from the logs:
  FAIL: fresh profile: the four agent surfaces agree (0)
  FAIL: after enabling one recipe the four agent surfaces agree (1)
  FAIL: after disabling that recipe the four agent surfaces agree (0) again

THE MECHANISM, per surface — three of them share a projection and the fourth does not
  Settings   options/options.js:2076-2080 → projectUnifiedAgents(named, enabledBackground)
  hub count  ntp/ntp.js:1240 refreshAgentCount → the same projection (lib/named-agents.js:1123)
  hub sidebar ntp/ntp.js:1174 renderSidebarAgents(agents) → fed by that same projection
  picker     sidepanel/sidepanel.html:189 `<agent-picker id="agents-picker" label="Agents"
             callable-only>` → components.js:9385 _visibleGroups() → filterGroups(
             agent-registry.js:93) with callableOnly/excludeRef/excludeId/query and NOTHING ELSE,
             over the four groups the registry returns (service-worker.js:7795-7838).
So the picker is not applying a different rule about acp; it is applying no kind rule at all. acp
rows are `{id, kind:"acp", name}` with no `enabled` field (service-worker.js:7833), and
isCallable's acp arm is `agent.enabled !== false` (agent-registry.js:82) → undefined !== false →
true, on every profile, unconditionally. `callable-only` therefore keeps all three, always.

THREE THINGS THE BEAD'S (a)/(b) FRAMING DOES NOT YET CONTAIN

1. The side panel already has a designed place for harnesses, and it is not the thing being counted.
   sidepanel.html:188 renders `<div class="harness-quick" id="harness-quick">` immediately ABOVE the
   picker at :189, both inside `#agents-list-pane`, populated by renderHarnessQuick()
   (sidepanel.js:71-108) — whose own comment says reaching pi/Claude Code/Codex "is a single click
   rather than a search" and that it reads "the SAME agent.registry authority the picker uses (no
   second list to keep in sync)". Its buttons carry class `hq`, not `.opt`, so the journey never
   counts them. Net effect today: the same three harnesses are offered twice in one panel — once as
   the affordance someone designed on purpose, once as a side effect of a filter that does not
   filter by kind. Any decision about the picker should be made knowing the designed affordance
   already exists and will keep existing.

2. The picker is wider than the invariant by more than acp — INFERENCE, NOT MEASURED, and it needs a
   journey to prove it. The registry also carries a `site` group (service-worker.js:7822) and
   isCallable returns true for site agents (agent-registry.js:83, "enrolled Site Agents are always
   callable"), while Settings and the hub project named + enabled background only. So the first
   scenario that enrols a site agent and then compares surfaces should reproduce this divergence
   with acp removed entirely. I checked and no current journey enrols a site agent before measuring
   surfaces, which is why this has stayed invisible. It is worth knowing before anyone treats (b) as
   "one kind, one filter, done".

3. One of the four comparisons is already blind to this. The scheduled-template check
   (chrome-journeys.ts:2558-2560) asserts sidebar 2 / panel 2 / settings 2 and does not assert
   sidepanelRows — which measured 5 in the same run. It passes. So the four-surfaces invariant is
   enforced on three of four surfaces that share it, and the +3 has been walking through the fourth
   unnoticed. Whatever rule Paul picks, that assertion wants extending, or the next divergence of
   this shape gets the same free pass.

WHAT EACH OPTION COSTS, MEASURED AGAINST THE CODE AS IT STANDS
(a) harnesses are agents, so the picker is right: then the other three surfaces have to show them
    too, and the fresh profile can never read "No agents yet." again — a string asserted at
    chrome-journeys.ts:1481 and 1484, plus the first-run copy checks that lean on it. That is a
    visible change to what a new owner sees on first run, not just a test update. Also: on a fresh
    install those three rows cannot run, so first run would show three agents that always fail.
(b) harnesses are not agents in the picker: not a one-attribute change, and the bead's wording
    implies it is. `filterGroups` accepts no `kinds` option (agent-registry.js:93) and
    `<agent-picker>` exposes no such attribute, so either the component grows one or the side panel
    stops using auto mode and passes two groups explicitly. Small — one component plus one call
    site — no change to the other three surfaces, and the fresh-profile empty state stays honest.
(c) not offered in the bead, and the numbers above are what surface it: keep the rows but gate them
    on availability. Today the group is emitted from a literal with no check for an installed native
    host or a running bridge, so the three rows exist on a machine that cannot use them. The failure
    at least tells the truth: acp-runner.js:568-580 names both remedies
    ("npm run acp:native:install" / "npm run acp:bridge") under category "harness-connection". If
    (c) is chosen, the availability probe it needs does not exist yet — I found no host-installed
    check anywhere in the registry path.

MY RECOMMENDATION, offered as a reading of the evidence rather than a decision
The counts say this was never a disagreement about acp. It is four surfaces implementing one idea in
four places, three of which call a shared projection and one of which calls the raw registry. On
that reading (b) matches what the code already treats as the projection, and (c) is what makes the
picker truthful on a machine without a harness — and the two are compatible: (b) now, availability
gate as a follow-up. Two things should ride along whichever way Paul calls it, because both are
independent of the decision: extend the scheduled-template assertion to cover the picker (finding 3),
and settle whether the picker's site rows are in the invariant (finding 2) before a scenario
discovers the answer by going red.

title: A 370-check load-sensitive gate has no owning issue: its beads closed and nothing noticed, so a lifecycle defect sat behind an unowned harness
description:
Found while chasing the journey abort at 132/370 (chrome-agent-platform-9t1p).

THE FACT PATTERN: scripts/chrome-journeys.ts is the most load-sensitive gate in the repo (370 sequential CDP round-trips, the reason quiet-window.ts and the fleet-wide heavy-gate slot exist), and the block it aborts in is owned by NOBODY:
- chrome-agent-platform-gsyp (CAP-FB-20260830-KEYLESS-FIRST-RESULT-01, 'A first result with no key') — CLOSED 2026-09-02, 'Completed and merged (migrated from TASKS-DONE.md)'. That is the bead the keyless block's checks were written for.
- chrome-agent-platform-xqhz (CAP-FB-20260830-EXEC-DEMO-01, the demo umbrella that path served) — CLOSED.
- CAP-FB-20260830-COOKIE-TOOLS-CUT-01 — NO BEAD AT ALL; the id exists only as a comment in the harness source (bd list --desc-contains returns nothing).
Searches for keyless / cookie value reader / COOKIE-TOOLS-CUT / DENIAL-TO-GRANT-CARD across every live state return only 9t1p (the fix I filed) and ady6 (a composer-selector migration in the same file — a mechanical task, not journey semantics).

WHY IT MATTERS, in one line: the block's checks outlived the bead they were written for, and nothing noticed — which is how a harness ends up running a silent 120-second wait for something whose owner stopped existing in September, and how a lifecycle defect stayed hidden behind an environmental classification nobody could question (see 9t1p and the qk7p comment of 2026-09-23).

ACCEPTANCE:
1. A gate or load-sensitive harness CARRIES AN OWNER that outlives the bead it was written for. The registry already holds the machinery for this shape — scripts/lib/harness-registry.ts records the loadSensitive declaration and expected-red OWNERS via its RED(verdict, reason, owner) helper — so the natural fix is an owner field beside loadSensitive, set for chrome-journeys and the KAT batch, with a guard (same shape as tests/quiet-window.test.ts's loadSensitive set check) that every load-sensitive entry names a live owning bead.
2. The guard FAILS when an owning bead closes while the harness stays load-sensitive — i.e. closing the owner is not a way to drop the responsibility silently.
3. 9t1p and the keyless/cookie-tools block are assigned to a NAMED owner in the same pass (coord is doing this: the semantic owner, not the file-proximity owner).

NOT THIS BEAD: the lifecycle defect itself (9t1p) and the composer-selector migration (ady6). This one is about the ownership hole that let both sit.

CORRECTION NOTE (same session, 2026-09-23): the first write of this description was mangled by the shell — backticked identifiers were command-substituted away, leaving gaps like 'records  declarations and expected-red OWNERS ()'. It was rewritten from stdin with a quoted heredoc; the text above is the intact version. Recorded rather than silently edited because a description with holes is exactly the blank where a reader assumes something was meant.

title: Every negative assertion in a security gate needs a positive counterpart proving there was something to be negative about — audit criterion after nweh
description:
Follow-on from chrome-agent-platform-nweh, filed rather than done blind because the sweep is wider than one gate and coord's instruction was to file it if large.

THE CRITERION, extracted from a defect that survived a green gate: a check of the form `!X.includes(bad)` or `count === 0` or `!/"value"/.test(text)` passes on EMPTY, ABSENT or NEVER-FETCHED data exactly as happily as it passes on clean data. It is only a check if a SIBLING assertion proves the payload was non-empty and the thing that should have produced it actually ran. In nweh both halves were missing at once: the fixture returned zero cookie rows (and Array.isArray([]) is true), and the regex could not have matched its own text because the text was double-stringified. The production mapper was correct the whole time — the instrument could not see a leak, and it was the gate whose subject is credential leakage.

The fix pattern that worked, and which is the template for the rest: THREE checks where there was one — (a) a POSITIVE check that the fixture was non-empty and the seeded marker reached the code under test, (b) the negative property asserted on DECODED structure rather than on a stringified blob, (c) the marker absent from every message that crossed the boundary, not just the last one. Then falsify by mutating production and requiring (b) and (c) to redden SPECIFICALLY while (a) and the plumbing check stay green — a differential, not just a red.

WHAT I VERIFIED, and what I did not. Bounded static pass over scripts/security-suite.ts only:
- The cookie section now has the pairing (checks at :497, :516, :527, :537). Measured: pristine 21/0, and the production mutant reddens exactly the two redaction checks.
- The negative assertions I found elsewhere in that file and did NOT verify: "network exfil: no request escaped the sandbox" and "network exfil: still zero after settle" (both count-based negatives; the four cap:fetch refusal checks look like their positive counterpart, but I did not prove the probes executed rather than failed to fire), "sandbox escape: window.opener is null", "prompt-injection: no chrome.runtime (extension API) in the sandbox" (absence of an API in a page — needs proof the sandbox document actually executed), and "sandbox escape: the outer page did not navigate away". LABEL: static reading, not measured. Each needs the same question asked of it: what positive fact proves there was something to be negative about?
- NOT SWEPT AT ALL: the other security-shaped gates and harnesses (scripts/security-injection.ts, scripts/security-suite-custody.mjs's own self-tests, the KATs, kat-webmcp-honest-errors.ts, and the ~40 harnesses in scripts/). The criterion is general; the sweep is not done.

METHOD FOR WHOEVER TAKES IT: for each check whose condition is a negative or a zero-count, write down the positive fact that must be true for the negative to mean anything, then look for that fact in the same run's assertions. If it is not there, add it as its own check (nweh's (a) is the model) and falsify the pair by mutating production, requiring the negative to redden while the positive stays green. Do not weaken or delete a negative to make a suite pass; a negative that cannot fail is the finding.

WHY THIS IS P2 AND NOT P3: a green check on a security property is the most expensive kind of reassurance there is. Tonight two gates inside test:all were red on main and a third (this one) was green while asserting nothing; the green one is the dangerous case, because it is the one nobody goes looking at.

title: Custody teardown crashes on ENOENT when the runner child has already exited: readProcIdentity reads /proc/<pid>/stat unguarded, so the run leaves NO receipt at all
description:
OBSERVED, not inferred. I launched npm run test:security and then killed it from outside (my own error: a pkill whose pattern matched more than I intended, during a run I should not have started while a flock -n check in the same command batch was reporting the lock held). The supervisor did not report a kill — it CRASHED:

  node:internal/fs/promises:1345
  Error: ENOENT: no such file or directory, open '/proc/3756057/stat'
      at async readFile (node:internal/fs/promises:1996:14)
      at async Promise.all (index 0)
      at async readProcIdentity (scripts/security-suite-custody.mjs:61:27)
      at async terminateAttestedGroup (scripts/security-suite-custody.mjs:326:21)
      at async scripts/security-suite-supervisor.mjs:344:17
  Node.js v24.21.0

The lock HAD been acquired normally first (CAP_SECURITY_LOCK_WAIT 1790119648220 / CAP_SECURITY_LOCK_ACQUIRED 1790119648299 — a 79 ms wait), so this is not a lock defect.

THE DEFECT: readProcIdentity reads /proc/<pid>/stat for a process that has already exited, and the ENOENT is not caught. That is a TOCTOU race inherent to the design — the group is scanned, then each member's identity is read, and a member can exit in between. It does not require an outside kill: any runner that dies on its own during teardown (a crash, an OOM kill, its own timeout firing at the same moment) can hit it.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN A CRASH: the supervisor's whole job is to leave an attested verdict. When this throws, there is NO CAP_SECURITY_RESULT line and NO receipt.json — the evidence directory is left without the record that says what happened. So the failure mode erases its own evidence, which is the same shape as the rest of tonight's defects: an exit-124 timeout hiding a FAIL printed 100 s earlier (bead im52), a swallowed page exception turning a missing element into a product accusation (bead 0lb4), a harness crashing before any check runs while its registry row still asserts a verdict (bead cwy2). A gate that cannot report how it died is a gate whose death gets attributed to the environment.

Note the contrast, which is why I am filing this as narrow rather than as a custody redesign: the 120 s TIMEOUT path handled the same situation correctly earlier tonight — receipt written with timedOut:true, termSent:true, residue [], cleaned true, groupSurvived false. So the attestation machinery works when the supervisor drives the termination and fails when the child is already gone.

FIX SHAPE: make readProcIdentity tolerate a vanished pid — return a distinguished "already-exited" identity rather than throwing — and make terminateAttestedGroup treat that as the benign case it is (the process is gone, which is what termination wanted), while still recording it in the receipt so the run says "child exited before identity read" instead of saying nothing. Keep the fail-closed behaviour for every OTHER error: an unreadable /proc for a process that still EXISTS must not be silently treated as exited, or the custody chain loses the ability to tell "it died" from "I could not see it".

ACCEPTANCE: kill the runner child from outside mid-run and get a receipt with a verdict rather than a Node stack trace and an evidence directory with no CAP_SECURITY_RESULT; the existing timeout path still produces its current receipt shape unchanged; a unit test covers both branches (pid vanished -> benign and recorded; pid present but unreadable -> still fail-closed).

REPRO: start npm run test:security, kill the runner child (not the supervisor) after CAP_SECURITY_LOCK_ACQUIRED, read stderr. Evidence of my instance: /tmp/cap8-sec-pristine.log. The clean re-run that followed waited for the lock and produced receipts normally (runId 72e9f4e6e938d4e8), so this did not leave the lock or the tree in a bad state — verified NOW-FREE afterwards and the worktree clean.

comments.author: Paul Kinlan
comments.text:
CANDIDATE PUSHED — branch cap/8ixk-custody-enoent @ 18c6e01c2e9d5aaebd69e2c14091a82da971a1fd, based on origin/main d31158b0. Worktree /home/paulkinlan/worktrees/cap-8ixk-custody, clean, check:dist clean at HEAD. 3 files: scripts/security-suite-custody.mjs, scripts/security-suite-supervisor.mjs, tests/security-suite-custody.test.ts. No product code, and the commit subject is prefixed `internal:` so the post-commit hook bailed and consumed no version — verified: package.json is still 0.3.475 and CHANGELOG's top entry is unrelated. That is ku6o's hook fix working end to end on a real internal commit.

MECHANISM, refined from what I filed. I originally described this as readProcIdentity being unguarded, which is true but is not where the crash escapes. The ENOENT IS caught: terminateAttestedGroup's catch calls procIdentities(), filters by pgid, and when the group is empty — exactly the case where everything already exited — `rows.length === 0` RETHROWS the original ENOENT. So the benign outcome (nothing left to terminate) took the fail-closed exit, escaped the supervisor as an uncaught rejection, and the run wrote no receipt. Fixing only readProcIdentity would have left the rethrow in place.

FIX, at the teardown site rather than in readProcIdentity, so that function's strict contract stays intact for its other three callers (attestOwnedGroup, procIdentities, and the supervisor's parent/self reads):
- new exported isVanishedProcError(error): true ONLY for code === "ENOENT". An unreadable /proc for a process that still exists is a different fact and is not laundered into "it exited" — that was the acceptance condition I wrote when filing this, and it is the reason the predicate is exported and unit-tested rather than inlined.
- terminateAttestedGroup's catch returns a distinguished benign result when the error is a vanished /proc AND the group is also gone. BOTH conditions are required and that conjunction is the fail-closed boundary: a dead leader inside a LIVE group still falls through to the observed-descendant ownership check and can still throw.
- readIdentity and isAlive became injectable options defaulting to readProcIdentity and groupAlive, the same pattern attestOwnedGroup already uses. Without them the race can only be tested by timing a real process death, and a flaky test of a teardown race is worse than none.
- the supervisor threads leaderExited into `termination` and sets custodyReason ||= "leader-exited-before-identity-read", so the receipt SAYS the child exited before the identity read instead of saying nothing. `||=` so it can never displace a real custody finding.

VERIFIED IT CANNOT CHANGE A VERDICT, which was the risk of touching a receipt field: exits 70/71/72 are gated on termination.survived, residue.length and cleanup.ok alone (security-suite-supervisor.mjs:385-387) and custodyReason is not consulted for the exit code. Confirmed empirically too — a real npm run test:security at this sha returned {"result":"PASS","exit":0,"timedOut":false,"termSent":false,"killSent":false,"groupSurvived":false,"residue":[],"custodyReason":"","cleaned":true} with runner.log RESULT: 21 passed, 0 failed. So the benign marker does not fire spuriously on a normal run and the happy path still writes its receipt.

TESTS: five added to tests/security-suite-custody.test.ts (17 passed / 0 failed in that file). The race is INJECTED, not timed, and the pgid/pid are impossible values so no path can reach process.kill:
- isVanishedProcError accepts only ENOENT; EACCES, ENOTDIR, a plain Error, null and undefined are all false.
- vanished leader + dead group -> {termSent:false, killSent:false, survived:false, leaderExited:true}, returned not thrown.
- vanished leader + group STILL ALIVE -> rejects, so the benign path provably needs both facts.
- EACCES + dead group -> rejects under the SAME alive sequence as the benign case, proving the gate is the error kind and not merely the group being gone.
- an identity CHANGE (starttime differs) -> still rejects with "owned process-group identity changed", so the pre-existing ownership check survives the new early return.

FALSIFICATION, as a differential. First attempt removed the whole benign block and was killed at TYPE level (dropping the return removed leaderExited from the inferred type, so the test did not type-check) — a kill, but not the one that proves the behavior. Redone as `if (false && ...)` so the return type is preserved and only the BEHAVIOR is removed: 16 passed / 1 FAILED, and the one red is exactly "a leader that vanished while its group also died is benign, returned and RECORDED — not rethrown", with the ENOENT visibly propagating. The four fail-closed tests stayed GREEN, so the mutant did not red the file by breaking something else. Committed BEFORE mutating, because an earlier attempt of mine restored a mutant with `git checkout --` over uncommitted work and discarded the fix along with it.

GATES at 18c6e01c: npm run test:changed exit 0 (fail-closed on scripts/security-suite-supervisor.mjs, which no test imports, and ran the full suite: 495 files, wall 440s); npm test exit 0 — serial phase 17 files GREEN 337s + parallel phase 478 files GREEN 85s, 495 files total, wall 422s, zero failures; npm run test:security exit 0 as above; build rc=0; check:dist clean. All five 8ixk tests verified BY NAME inside the full suite, not only in isolation.

NOT DONE, and deliberately: I did not attempt to reproduce the original crash by killing a live runner mid-run. That needs a real test:security run to interrupt, which means holding the canonical lock and then deliberately breaking a gate run for the fleet; the injected tests cover both branches deterministically, which is stronger evidence than one timed reproduction. If the reviewer wants the live reproduction anyway, the recipe is in the bead description (start npm run test:security, kill the runner child after CAP_SECURITY_LOCK_ACQUIRED, read stderr).

comments.text:
REVISION PUSHED addressing all of cap-astra's finalized REVISE findings on 18c6e01c. Branch cap/8ixk-custody-enoent now at 285c3adb00d785141cefc594ceb43592a452bea1, three commits on base d31158b0: 18c6e01c (the original ENOENT guard, credited as working by review), 4092e2f5 (finding 2), 285c3adb (finding 3). Reviewer's report: ~/cap-evidence/8ixk-astra-review-20260924/REVIEW.md. Author evidence with MANIFEST: ~/cap-evidence/8ixk-author-evidence/.

FINDING 2 — EARLY-EXIT COMPLETENESS (4092e2f5). Review reproduced with a LIVE owned fixture at the unchanged 18c6e01c: both kernel identity reads complete, the own child then dies before completion is delivered, and process.kill(-pgid, SIGTERM) throws killESRCH — escaping uncaught, Node exit 1, NO receipt. A pre-existing sibling of the ENOENT race, not newly introduced, but the acceptance is "an early exit leaves a receipt", which guarding one read does not deliver. Fixed: both process.kill calls tolerate ESRCH (a group that finished dying between the alive check and the signal is the outcome termination wanted) and return a distinguished groupGoneBeforeSignal result. ONLY ESRCH qualifies — EPERM and every other kill failure still propagate, because not being ALLOWED to signal a group is a real custody finding and must not be laundered into "it already exited". isVanishedGroupError is exported and unit-tested for exactly that boundary. `kill` became injectable so no test ever signals a real group (an impossible pgid is inside the pid range on some kernels). The supervisor additionally wraps teardown in terminateAttestedGroupSafely, so the no-lost-receipt property is now STRUCTURAL rather than an enumeration of the races I thought of — which is the point, since review found one I had not. It records teardownThrew in the receipt and deliberately does NOT change any exit code; whether a non-ESRCH teardown refusal should also force a non-zero exit is a policy call for the desk, and today the refusal is at least visible instead of erasing the receipt.

FINDING 3 — CALLER COVERAGE AND CLEANUP DIAGNOSTIC PRIORITY (285c3adb). Two things, the second a REGRESSION I INTRODUCED. (a) A caller-only mutant, `if (false && termination.leaderExited)` in the supervisor, survived all 17 custody tests because every test asserted what the HELPER RETURNS and nothing asserted what the RECEIPT RECORDS; review's live probe confirmed custodyReason came back empty where it should have said leader-exited-before-identity-read. My own commit message had claimed the marker was "recorded" — the helper returned it and nothing downstream was tested. (b) I assigned the benign markers BEFORE the cleanup check, and cleanup used `||=`, so it could no longer replace them: a run with both a benign leader exit and a private-profile symlink refusal reported custodyReason=leader-exited-before-identity-read at exit 71 with cleaned:false (receipt b21e2e6180fb0ca9), where the control with only the marker assignment disabled reported the proper cleanup-refused:profile is not an owned regular directory (d09361b8bf36e32c). The exit code failed closed correctly throughout, so this was a WRONG DIAGNOSTIC rather than a wrong verdict — and it is precisely what my own code comment promised could not happen ("must never displace a real custody finding"). Only a live fixture caught it; no unit test covered the order at all. Fixed by making the derivation ONE pure exported function, custodyReasonFor({survived, residueCount, cleanupOk, cleanupReason, leaderExited, groupGoneBeforeSignal, teardownThrew}), called by the supervisor once AFTER cleanup. The order is the semantics, so it now lives in one testable place instead of in the sequence of mutations applied to a local. Precedence most-severe-first: descendant-residue, owned-group-survived, cleanup-refused, teardown-threw, then the two benign races. The first three are byte-for-byte the pre-8ixk behaviour (residue overwrote survived; cleanup only filled an empty reason); the benign markers are new and go last, which is what fixes the regression.

TESTS: 25 passed / 0 failed in tests/security-suite-custody.test.ts (12 pre-existing, 5 for the ENOENT race, 4 for the ESRCH race, 4 for the derivation). New derivation tests: a clean run records no reason; each of the six findings records its own; THE REGRESSION CASE — benign marker plus cleanup refusal — records cleanup-refused for all three benign markers; and the full severity order is pinned including residue-overwrites-survived, survived-not-replaced-by-cleanup, threw-outranks-benign and first-benign-wins.

FALSIFICATION, three mutants, each committed BEFORE mutating:
- ENOENT helper mutant (`if (false && isVanishedProcError(...) && !isAlive(...))`, return type preserved): 16/1, the single red the benign-case test, four fail-closed tests green.
- ESRCH mutant (`if (true) throw error` at both kill sites): 19/2, reds exactly the two ESRCH tests, EPERM and all ENOENT tests green.
- Derivation mutant (`if (false && leaderExited)` inside custodyReasonFor): 23/2, reds "each finding records its own reason" and the severity-order test. Restored: 25/0.
- One mutant attempt was DISCARDED and is kept in the evidence: deleting the whole benign block was killed at TYPE level only (the inferred return type lost leaderExited, so the test stopped type-checking), which proves nothing about behaviour. A second attempt used wrong quoting and silently ran against the UNMUTATED file, reporting 25/0 — caught because a mutant that reports all-green is a contradiction, and re-run properly.

COVERAGE BOUNDARY, stated rather than rounded up: the new tests pin the DERIVATION. The WIRING — the supervisor passing termination.leaderExited and the rest into custodyReasonFor — is still covered only by review's live owned-fixture probe, because the supervisor is a top-level script that cannot be imported without running it. A caller-only mutant of the wiring would still survive these unit tests. That probe is the correct instrument for the wiring and should be re-run against 285c3adb; I am not claiming unit coverage I do not have.

GATES AT 285c3adb, all re-run: npm test exit 0 — serial phase 17 files GREEN 225s + parallel phase 478 files GREEN 52s, 495 files total, wall 277s, zero failures, all 8ixk tests present by name in the suite log; npm run test:security exit 0 with receipt {"result":"PASS","exit":0,"timedOut":false,"termSent":false,"killSent":false,"groupSurvived":false,"residue":[],"custodyReason":"","cleaned":true} and runner.log RESULT: 21 passed, 0 failed — custodyReason EMPTY on a normal run, so neither benign marker fires spuriously; npm run build:production rc=0; npm run check:dist clean at HEAD; canonical lock verified FREE before the security run and the worktree clean after. Receipts preserved durably under ~/cap-evidence/8ixk-author-evidence/security-run-*/.

comments.text:
REVISION 2 PUSHED — cap/8ixk-custody-enoent @ 7de4802de8a10c68c1ad26bdb7eeffc29afa32a8 (four commits on d31158b0: 18c6e01c, 4092e2f5, 285c3adb, 7de4802d). Addresses cap-astra's two points on 285c3adb, and the first is a LOOSENING I SHIPPED BY INFERENCE.

1. FAIL-CLOSED TREATMENT OF A GENUINE REFUSAL, RESTORED. terminateAttestedGroupSafely catches a teardown throw so the receipt is still written, but it did not restore the exit code. Before this bead's work an EPERM or identity-change refusal escaped as an uncaught rejection: supervisor exit 1, no receipt. After it, the same refusal produced a receipt with custodyReason=teardown-threw:... and the RUNNER's exit code — which is 0 when the run itself passed. So a real custody refusal had become a pass-with-a-note. My previous commit message said the change 'deliberately does NOT change any exit code', which was true about not adding a change and FALSE IN EFFECT, because the previous behaviour was a non-zero exit. Review is right that any new potentially-successful teardown refusal needs explicit review or owner decision rather than inferred policy approval, so this restores the prior fail-closed outcome verbatim rather than re-deciding it: exitCode becomes 1 when teardownThrew is set and the run would otherwise have exited 0. Applied only in that case so a runner's own failure code is never masked. Whether a dedicated code in the 70/71/72 family is better than 1 is flagged as a desk/owner decision and NOT taken.

2. CALLER-LEVEL COVERAGE, AND MY 'UNIMPORTABLE' CLAIM WAS WRONG. I had declared the supervisor untestable because it is a top-level script. This test file already spawns it via runSupervisor with the self-test fixture and parses CAP_SECURITY_RESULT, and has done so for the guard, pgid-mismatch, timeout, stubborn, exit37, signal and escape scenarios. So the wiring was testable all along and I called an instrument a blocker. Added a caller-level test: a real TERM teardown writes its receipt, records termSent:true, and records NO benign custody marker. Without it, a change that made the benign markers fire on any termination would pass every unit test, because the unit tests pin custodyReasonFor's derivation and not what the supervisor passes into it.

COVERAGE BOUNDARY, stated rather than rounded up. The caller-level test covers the NEGATIVE direction. Two things it does not cover, neither hidden by it: (a) a benign marker actually reaching the receipt needs a fixture scenario where the leader vanishes or the group dies before the signal — none of the existing scenarios does, so the positive direction is still covered only by the reviewer's live owned fixture probe; (b) the restored fail-closed exit for teardownThrew cannot be driven end to end either, because no fixture scenario produces a teardown throw and no CAP_SECURITY_TEST_* hook forces one (the hooks are ESCAPE_CHILD_FAIL, FORCE_ATTEST_MISMATCH, SAMPLE_FREEZE_MS, SCENARIO, STATE). Adding such a hook means putting test-only surface into production code, which is a reviewed change and not one to make unilaterally at the end of a revision. The invariant is asserted as 'a run that exits 0 must not be carrying a custody finding', which is weaker than driving it and is labelled as such.

TESTS: 26 passed / 0 failed in tests/security-suite-custody.test.ts (was 25); the new one spawns the real supervisor in 513ms and asserts against its parsed receipt.

GATES AT 7de4802d, all re-run: npm test exit 0 — parallel phase 478 files GREEN 71s, 495 files total, wall 275s, zero failures; npm run test:security exit 0 with receipt {"result":"PASS","exit":0,"custodyReason":""} and runner.log RESULT: 21 passed, 0 failed, so neither benign marker fires spuriously on a normal run; build rc=0; check:dist clean at HEAD; canonical lock FREE and worktree clean. Receipts preserved under ~/cap-evidence/8ixk-author-evidence/security-run-rev4-*/.

PROCESS NOTE, recorded because it nearly cost a gate: the first commit of this revision had its message polluted by an unterminated heredoc that swallowed the trailing shell commands, and the gate chain in that same command therefore NEVER LAUNCHED. Caught by checking whether the gates had actually run rather than assuming the command succeeded — /tmp/cap33.done was absent and no gates log existed. COVERAGE GAPS KEPT EXPLICIT for the next review, plus a correction to my own boundary claim (cap-astra seq164).

CORRECTION — MY 'NEEDS A PRODUCTION HOOK' CLAIM WAS WRONG. I wrote that driving the positive direction and the fail-closed refusal end to end would require putting test-only surface into production code, and therefore was not a change to make unilaterally. cap-astra is right that it is not: the supervisor's self-test path already spawns a FIXTURE runner (CAP_SECURITY_RUNNER=tests/fixtures/security-suite-fake-runner.mjs) selected by CAP_SECURITY_TEST_SCENARIO, and that fixture already drives timeout, stubborn, escape, guard, pgid-mismatch, exit37 and signal. A new scenario in that fixture — a child that dies after the identity read but before completion is delivered, and one that provokes a genuine refusal — is TEST-SUPPORT CODE ONLY. No production hook is needed, and cap-astra's own durable probes already demonstrate the pre/post-identity-death and genuine-refusal cases with a test-support preload around the existing owned fixture. So the gap is closable without touching shipped code, and my reason for not closing it does not hold.

STILL OPEN, AND DELIBERATELY NOT CLAIMED AS COVERED:
1. POSITIVE CALLER COVERAGE (the original R2). Nothing in the committed suite proves the benign flag actually REACHES the receipt on disk. tests/security-suite-custody.test.ts proves custodyReasonFor derives leader-exited-before-identity-read and group-gone-before-signal correctly, and the caller-level test proves a NORMAL teardown records NO benign marker. Negative marker coverage does not close R2: a supervisor that dropped termination.leaderExited on the way into custodyReasonFor would pass every committed test. Today that wiring is verified only by cap-astra's live owned-fixture probe (receipt 49cdbaf342180fa9, custodyReason leader-exited-before-identity-read, cleaned true) — reviewer-side evidence, not a shipped regression test.
2. FAIL-CLOSED REGRESSION COVERAGE. The restored exit-1-on-teardownThrew is asserted only as the invariant 'a run that exits 0 must not be carrying a custody finding'. No committed test drives a genuine refusal through the supervisor and asserts a non-zero exit, so a future change that re-loosens it would not be caught by the suite. This is the exact defect class I shipped once already at 285c3adb (fail-open on a genuine refusal), which is why it should not rest on an untestable-by-me claim.

SHAPE OF THE FIX, so the next lane does not re-derive it: add fixture scenarios that (a) let the child exit after both kernel identity reads complete but before completion is delivered — expect a receipt with custodyReason leader-exited-before-identity-read and the run's own exit code; (b) let the group die before the signal — expect group-gone-before-signal; (c) provoke a genuine refusal (EPERM or an identity change) — expect a NON-ZERO exit AND a receipt naming teardown-threw, which is the pairing that was broken at 285c3adb. All three are fixture-side. Then the reviewer's live probe becomes corroboration rather than the only coverage.

comments.author: Paul Kinlan
comments.text:
CORRECTION to the fixture-scenario labels in my previous comment, from cap-astra seq166 and verified against the shipped code. I recorded a WRONG expected marker, and a wrong expectation written on a bead is how a future lane encodes the wrong test — so it is corrected here rather than only in chat.

WHAT I GOT WRONG: I wrote that a child exiting 'after both identity reads complete but before completion is delivered' should expect custodyReason leader-exited-before-identity-read. It should expect **group-gone-before-signal**.

WHY, from the code at 7de4802d rather than from memory:
- leaderExited:true is returned at scripts/security-suite-custody.mjs:397, inside the catch guarded at :392 by . So it requires the IDENTITY READ ITSELF to throw ENOENT — the leader's /proc entry vanished before or during readProcIdentity — AND the group to be dead. That is cap-astra's BEFORE-identity probe.
- groupGoneBeforeSignal:true is returned at :427 and :442, inside the two kill guards . Reaching them means the identity read SUCCEEDED (the try completed, the identity matched), and then process.kill(-pgid, SIGTERM) or the SIGKILL escalation threw ESRCH because the group finished dying in between. That is the AFTER-identity case.

So the two markers are distinguished by WHICH syscall found the process gone — the /proc read or the signal — and a fixture scenario has to aim at one or the other deliberately. Encoding 'dies after the identity reads' as leader-exited-before-identity-read would have produced a test asserting a marker the code can never emit on that path, which would fail and invite someone to 'fix' it by weakening the assertion.

CORRECTED FIX SHAPE, replacing the one in my previous comment. Three fixture scenarios in tests/fixtures/security-suite-fake-runner.mjs (test-support code only, no production hook):
  (a) BEFORE-IDENTITY DEATH: the child exits so that readProcIdentity throws ENOENT while the group is also gone -> expect a receipt with custodyReason **leader-exited-before-identity-read** and the run's own exit code.
  (b) AFTER-IDENTITY DEATH: both kernel identity reads complete and their actual bytes are delivered, then the child/group dies before the signal lands, so process.kill raises ESRCH -> expect **group-gone-before-signal**.
  (c) GENUINE REFUSAL: provoke EPERM or an identity change (starttime/pgid/sid/uid mismatch) -> expect a **NON-ZERO exit AND a receipt naming teardown-threw:<message>**. That pairing is exactly what was broken at 285c3adb, where the receipt survived but the exit code did not.
After those three, cap-astra's live owned-fixture probe becomes corroboration rather than the only coverage of the wiring.

STATUS UNCHANGED AND NOT UPGRADED BY THIS CORRECTION: both coverage gaps in my previous comment remain open author acknowledgements — positive caller coverage (the benign flag actually reaching the receipt) and fail-closed regression coverage (a genuine refusal exiting non-zero). cap-astra records them as author reports with no new runtime approval, and 7de4802d remains a new author-reported candidate, not an approved one. Nothing here claims otherwise.

comments.author: Paul Kinlan
comments.text:
TEXT REPAIR for my previous comment: two code conditions were eaten by shell command substitution because I wrote them inside backticks, so that comment reads "inside the catch guarded at :392 by ." and "inside the two kill guards" with the predicate missing. A bead comment with the condition silently deleted is worse than no comment, since it still looks authoritative. The substance of the correction is unchanged; only the two predicates are restated here, without backticks.

Predicate 1 — the leaderExited path, scripts/security-suite-custody.mjs:392 guarding the return at :397:
    if (isVanishedProcError(error) && !isAlive(pgid))
So leader-exited-before-identity-read requires BOTH that the identity read itself threw ENOENT (isVanishedProcError is true only for code === "ENOENT") AND that the group is already dead. This is the BEFORE-identity case.

Predicate 2 — the groupGoneBeforeSignal paths, the kill guards at :422 and :437 guarding the returns at :427 and :442:
    if (!isVanishedGroupError(error)) throw error;
So group-gone-before-signal is reached only when the identity read SUCCEEDED and the try block completed, and then process.kill(-pgid, SIGTERM) or the SIGKILL escalation threw ESRCH (isVanishedGroupError is true only for code === "ESRCH"). Every other kill failure is rethrown, which is what keeps an EPERM refusal fail-closed. This is the AFTER-identity case.

The distinction the correction turns on, restated plainly: the two markers are separated by WHICH syscall found the process gone — the /proc identity read, or the signal. A fixture scenario must aim at one deliberately, and encoding "dies after the identity reads" as leader-exited-before-identity-read would assert a marker the code cannot emit on that path.

The fix is mechanical — pass bead text through a single-quoted heredoc, or avoid backticks entirely — and the check is to read the stored comment back rather than trusting the tool's success line, which is how both were caught.

title: Take the fleet-wide gate turn in the remaining gate-class harnesses — read the custody fd-9 protocol first, because a second lock is how you get a deadlock neither lock can see
description:
Follow-up from chrome-agent-platform-0lj3 (the fleet-wide heavy-gate slot). Landed scope there: chrome-journeys.ts and scripts/kat-runner.ts take the turn through launchChrome's fleetSlot/requireQuiet pairing. NOT done there, deliberately:

1. The other gate-class entries in scripts/lib/harness-registry.ts still take only a browser slot (or their own scope) and can therefore run concurrently with a journey: the a11y gate (scripts/a11y-audit.ts, npm test:a11y), the components gate (scripts/component-gallery-smoke.ts, npm test:components), the width gate (scripts/npm run test:width), and the named on-demand suites that drive many browsers.
2. The security custody chain (scripts/security-suite-supervisor.sh + scripts/security-suite-supervisor.sh's fd-9 to the canonical lock, guarded by tests/security-suite-custody.test.ts) must be READ before anything else is layered onto its exclusivity.

THE CAUTION, in coord's words (2026-09-22), because it is the acceptance condition and not a note: 'A second lock introduced into a system that already has one is how you get a deadlock neither lock can see.' Concretely for this work: a harness that takes the heavy-gate slot and then requests the canonical lock (or vice versa) can wait on itself if the ordering is not fixed; the security supervisor already holds the canonical lock on fd 9 for its whole run, so a naive 'wrap everything in the heavy slot' would add a second wait to a process that is already a lock holder. Fix the ORDER first (one documented acquisition order across the fleet), then wire.

ACCEPTANCE: each gate-class entry either takes the fleet turn (verified by the same two-way guard 0lj3 uses: registry declaration set == sources passing fleetSlot) or carries a recorded reason why it deliberately does not, with the deadlock analysis for the custody chain written down. Plus: a test that a process holding the heavy-gate slot and then asking for the canonical lock cannot self-deadlock (bounded wait + named holder, whichever order is chosen).

1. THE DEADLOCK CAUTION, IN CODE. The system already has one lock — scripts/security-suite-supervisor.sh holds the canonical serialized-Chrome lock on fd 9 for its whole run (exec 9>"$LOCK"; flock -x 9) and launches its harnesses as children.
